activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: Small children sometimes sit on a booster seat so the hairdresser can reach their hair.
story:
Nolan was at Grandma's house. Today was a big day. "You get your first haircut!" said Grandma. Nolan clapped his hands. His hair had little curls. Soon they would be short and clean.

Grandma drove Nolan to the salon. A man named Sam smiled. "Hop up!" said Sam. The chair was very big. Nolan tried to sit. But Sam stood and looked and shook his head. "You are too short for the big chair," said Sam. "I cannot reach your hair from up here."

Nolan wanted his haircut. He wanted it now! Sam went away. He came back with something. It was a booster seat. It was like the one at the playground, but clean and red. Sam put it on the big chair. "Climb on," said Sam.

Nolan sat on the booster seat. Up, up he went! Now his head was high. Now Sam could reach his hair. Snip, snip went the scissors. Curly bits fell down. They landed on the floor like little clouds.

"All done!" said Sam. Nolan looked in the mirror. His curls were short. His hair was clean. "I sat on the booster seat!" said Nolan. Grandma hugged him tight.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: A scoreboard shows how many points each team has.
story:
Eliana sat on the big rug. The room smelled like warm popcorn. Everyone was watching the game on TV. Grandpa was in his soft chair. Mama and Papa sat on the couch.

"Who is winning?" Eliana asked. "Who has more points?"

"Can you remember the score?" asked Grandpa.

Eliana tried. She forgot the numbers. She pulled her teddy close.

Then Grandpa pointed up high. "See the scoreboard," he said. Eliana looked at the big bright board on the screen. It showed two teams. It showed numbers for each team. The red team had more points. The blue team had less.

"The red team is winning!" Eliana said.

The blue team ran fast. They kicked the ball. The crowd on TV got loud. Eliana looked back at the scoreboard. The blue numbers went up. Now the two teams had the same points.

"It changed!" said Eliana. "The scoreboard changed!"

She watched the board the whole time now. The door was closed so it was quiet and cozy.

Later the red team got one more point. Grandpa clapped his hands. Eliana clapped her teddy's paws.

"We won," said Grandpa.

Eliana pointed at the scoreboard and smiled. "The red team has the most points!"

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: On a traffic light, red means stop and green means go.
story:
Kai sat at the art table. It was a hot summer day. He wanted to make a traffic light for the class game.

First he found the red paint. He painted the top circle red. Then he painted the middle circle yellow. The bottom circle was green. His friend Mia painted a blue car for the game.

"Now we can play crossing the street," said Mia. She held the blue car up high. Kai held up the traffic light. He turned the red circle to the top.

"Red means stop," said Mia. The blue car stopped right away. Vroom. It sat so still.

Kai turned the green circle to the top. "Green means go," said Mia. The blue car went, "Zoom, zoom!" It went fast past the crayon box.

"What about yellow?" asked Kai. He turned the yellow circle to the top. Mia drove the car a little bit. Then she stopped it. "Yellow is in the middle," she said. "Not stop and not go."

Kai laughed. He wondered if a bad driver would mix up the colors. He held up red again. "Stop, stop!" he called. Mia stopped the car with a little screech.

At pickup time, Kai held his teacher's hand at the real crossing. The real light turned red. All the cars stopped. "Red means stop," said Kai. Then it turned green. The cars zipped by, one after another. Kai squeezed his teacher's hand and whispered, "Green means go."

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
fact: Many Christian families say grace, a short prayer of thanks, before meals.
story:
Emile was at Grandma's house. Dinner was hot on the table. There was warm soup and bread.

Emile wanted to eat right away. He grabbed his spoon. Grandma held up her hand. "Wait, Emile. First we say grace."

"What is grace?" asked Emile.

"It is a short prayer of thanks," said Grandma. "Many Christian families say it before meals. Would you like to say it?"

Emile nodded. He put down his spoon. He folded his little hands. "Thank you, God, for soup. Thank you for bread. Thank you for Grandma."

"Emile said it!" he cheered.

Grandma laughed and poured him some milk. "Very good. Now we can eat."

Emile took a big sip of soup. "Grace first, soup next!"

Grandma patted his hat. "That's right, my boy."

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A cube, like a toy block, has six flat faces, and each one is a square.
story:
Gabriella sat at the art table. She wanted to make a picture of a house. She had paper, crayons, and a box of stickers. But her house looked wrong. The roof would not sit on the walls.

Her friend Leo was there too. He had a toy block. "This is a cube," Leo said. "It has six flat faces." Gabriella picked up the block. She turned it over and over. She put a sticker on each flat face. One, two, three, four, five, six. Every face was a square, just like her stickers.

Gabriella looked at the block. Then she drew a square for her house. She drew a triangle for the roof. The triangle sat on the square just right. She drew a rectangle for the door. Then she drew a circle for the window. A paper rabbit crawled out of Leo's pocket and sat by her picture. "The rabbit wants to come in," Leo said. Gabriella drew a little square door just for him.

Then she washed her hands until they were clean. She hung her picture up high. "Look, a house!" she said. Leo clapped, and the rabbit ear wiggled.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
fact: After playing outside or petting an animal, it is time to wash your hands.
story:
Sienna ran outside to play. She patted the big red dog. "Soft fur!" she said. The dog wagged his tail. Then Mom called, "Lunch time!"

Sienna ran to the table. She reached for her sandwich. Mom shook her head. "You petted the dog. Hands first!" Sienna looked at her hands. They looked the same as before. But she ran to the sink anyway.

Mom turned on the water. Sienna pumped the soap. "Now we count to twenty," said Mom. "One, two, three..." Sienna rubbed her soapy hands. "Four, five, six..." Bubbles grew big and white. "Seven, eight, nine, ten..." They looked like clouds! "Eleven, twelve, thirteen..." Sienna lifted her hands up high. The bubbles wiggled. "Fourteen, fifteen!" A bubble floated off her thumb.

"A bubble is flying!" Sienna laughed. It popped in the air, far above her head. "Sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty!" Mom gave her a towel. Sienna dried her clean hands all by herself.

She ran back to the table and took a big bite. "Yum!" said Sienna. Then she held up her hands. "Dog fur all gone!" Mom clapped. "Wash them again after the toilet too," she said. "Twenty seconds, every time." Sienna grinned. "I can count to twenty!" At nap time, she whispered the numbers to her teddy on the bed. "One, two, three, four..."

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: Tiny bits of cut hair can feel itchy on your neck.
story:
Asher sat in the big barber chair. It went up, up, up! The barber put a cape on him. "First haircut!" said Mom. Asher smiled a big smile.

The barber picked up the scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. Some bits landed on Asher's neck. Asher wiggled. He wiggled some more. His neck felt itchy! "I don't like this," said Asher.

The barber got a soft brush. She brushed the little bits away. Whoosh, whoosh. The itch went away! Asher sat very still. "All done," said the barber. Asher jumped down and ran to Mom. "The brush made the itch go away!" he said. Mom clapped her hands. "What a big boy," she said. "I am so happy!" said Asher. At home, Dad would miss his little baby hair. But Asher did not miss it one bit. He touched his new short hair and grinned.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: Being fair means everyone gets a chance.
story:
Beatrice loved the big red blocks at school. She wanted to build a robot. A tall, nice robot with block arms.

At free play time, Beatrice ran to the block corner. Her friend Tom was already there. Tom grabbed all the blocks. He hugged them close. "They are all mine," said Tom. Beatrice had zero blocks. Her robot could not start.

Then Mia came over. Mia had zero blocks too. Tom sat alone with every block. Nobody could build with him. Tom looked around. He saw two sad friends and one full arm.

Tom put the blocks in the middle. "You take some. You take some. I keep some," he said. Beatrice got a big pile. Mia got a big pile. Tom got a big pile too. Everyone got a chance to build.

Beatrice stacked two blocks, then two more. Mia made legs for the robot. Tom gave it block arms. The robot grew tall. It was the nicest robot ever. Miss Kay came to look. "What a fine robot!" she said. Beatrice waved her hand at the robot. "We all built it," she said. "Everyone helped."

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: You see colors with your eyes; you cannot tell a color by feeling it with your fingers.
story:
Everett ran to the feely bag at daycare. "My turn!" he said. Teacher Mia held out the bag. Everett pushed his hand in. He felt something round. He felt something smooth. "A ball!" he said. "It is a red ball!"

"Are you sure it is red?" asked Teacher Mia. Everett pulled out the ball. It was blue! His friend Ana laughed. "You have to look," she said. "Your fingers cannot see colors." Ana took her turn next. She felt a soft square. "A cloth!" she said. "But I do not know the color yet." She peeked. The cloth was yellow!

Then Everett felt something bumpy in the bag. It was small and cold. He pulled it out. It was a green truck, so cute, with snow painted on top. "A green truck with snow on it!" he cheered. Ana clapped her hands. Teacher Mia smiled. "One more turn," she said. Everett reached into the bag with a big grin.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: We say "please" when we ask for something.
story:
Avery went to the store with Mama. The lights were bright. The carts went roll, roll, roll. Avery saw a big bin of apples. She wanted a red apple.

Avery grabbed for the apple. Another little boy was reaching too. His hand touched hers. He looked sad. Avery let go and waited. The boy took one apple. Then it was Avery's turn. She reached out again, but she grabbed fast.

"Say please when you ask for something," said Mama. Avery stopped her hand. "Please," said Avery. "May I have an apple?" Mama smiled. "Yes, you may." The man at the bin smiled too. He gave Avery a big red apple.

Avery held the apple in both hands. The boy came back. He had a small bread roll to share. Avery broke it and gave him half. "Thank you," said the boy. "You're welcome," said Avery. Then they walked down the pillow aisle together, and Avery patted one soft pillow. It was soft as a cloud. "Please can we touch one more?" said Avery. "One more," said Mama.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Taking slow, deep breaths can help your body calm down when you feel angry.
story:
Mia wanted her horse at bedtime. She looked under her bed. The horse was missing. Mia felt sad. She stomped her foot. "I am angry!" she said. Her tummy felt tight.

Mama came in. "Where is my horse?" Mia asked. "Let us look together," said Mama. They looked in the toy box. They looked by the window. Snow was falling outside, soft and slow. There was the horse, on the shelf! Mia felt excited. She hugged him tight.

Then she felt worried. "Will he be cold?" she asked. "No," said Mama. "He is warm and safe." Mia felt better. Mama sat close. "Try slow, deep breaths with me," she said. Mia breathed in slow. She breathed out slow. Her tummy felt soft. Her eyes felt sleepy. Mia yawned and held her horse all night.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: A child can greet a grandparent with a hug, a wave, or a hello.
story:
Grandma was coming to stay. Grandma would come for a whole week. Harrison stood by the door. He held his teddy bear tight.

"I want to hide," Harrison said.

Mom knelt down next to him. "You can give Grandma a big hug," she said. "Or you can wave. Or you can just say hello."

The car pulled up. Grandma got out. She had a big bag and a happy face. Harrison held his teddy tighter. His foot stayed on the bottom step. He was not ready for a hug yet.

So Harrison lifted his hand. He waved.

Grandma waved back. "Hello, Harrison!" she called. Her voice was warm like soup.

Harrison's tummy felt better. He came down one step. Then one more. He tapped his foot on the mat. "Hello, Grandma," he said, very small.

Grandma sat on the step beside him. She smelled like flowers. "Would you like to see what is in my bag?" she asked.

Harrison nodded. Grandma pulled out a soft blanket. It was blue and big.

Harrison put teddy on the blanket. Then Harrison leaned over. He gave Grandma a hug after all.

Grandma hugged him back. "Hello to you too," she whispered.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: You can often tell how a friend feels by looking at their face.
story:
Benjamin ran to the playground. He wanted to swing up high. The swing was his favorite thing. But then he saw his friend Milo on the bench. Milo sat all alone. His mouth was turned down. His eyes looked wet. Benjamin could tell how Milo felt just by looking at his face. Milo looked sad.

Benjamin walked over. "Why are you sad?" he asked. "My dog ran to the farm and I can't find him," said Milo. Just then a big dog came running. It barked very loud. Milo's face changed. His eyes got wide. He looked scared. "That bark was scary," said Milo. "But look," said Benjamin. "It is your dog! He came back from the farm!"

Milo smiled a big smile now. He jumped up and down. "I am so excited!" he said. Benjamin laughed. Then a big boy pushed past them and grabbed the swing. Benjamin's face got hot and red. He made two fists. He felt angry. But the big boy's face looked sorry. "Sorry," the boy said. "You can go first." Benjamin's fists opened. He felt happy again. He got on the swing. "Push me, Milo!" he called. Milo pushed, and up Benjamin went, high into the blue sky.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Fans cheer and clap when their team scores.
story:
Sarah sat with Mom and Dad at a big restaurant. A big screen hung on the wall. A game was on. Everyone at the tables watched it.

The players ran with the ball. Then one team kicked it in. The goal counted! The people near Sarah stood up. They clapped and cheered. "Why are they so loud?" Sarah asked. Dad smiled. "Watch. Their team just scored."

Then the other team ran fast. They kicked the ball in too. Sarah jumped up. She clapped hard and cheered, "Yay! Yay!" But no one else clapped. The people looked at her. Then Sarah looked at Dad. Dad was clapping for the other team! Sarah laughed and laughed. "Oops," she said. "I clapped for the wrong team!"

The waiter brought fries, and Sarah said sorry to Dad for the loud cheer. Dad laughed and gave her a big high five. Then their team scored again. This time Sarah and Dad stood up together. They clapped and cheered side by side.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: A new baby cannot talk yet, so it cries to show it needs something.
story:
Henry walked with Mom into the hospital. He held Dad's hand. They went to a big room with a bed. In the bed was a tiny baby. "That is your baby sister," said Mom.

The baby made a loud cry. "Waa! Waa!" Henry covered his ears. "Why is she crying?" he asked. Dad said, "A new baby cannot talk yet." Henry waited. The baby cried again. Dad gave her some milk. Then she stopped crying. Henry saw that. The cry asked for milk, and Dad gave it.

The baby cried one more time. Henry got a soft blanket. He put it near her, very slow. She stopped crying and made a small sound. "She talks with cries," said Henry. He gave his sister a kiss on her head. "I will listen to you," he said. The baby held his young finger tight.

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
fact: Sun, sock and sand all start with the letter S and the 'sss' sound.
story:
Brielle sat in her reading nook with a big alphabet book. She pointed at the letter S. "That one is tricky," she said.

Mom sat down next to her. "S says sss," said Mom. "Like a little snake."

Brielle looked around the nook. She wanted to find an S word all by herself. She saw her red sock on the floor. She held it up. "Sss sock!" she said. "Sock starts with S!" Mom clapped.

Then sun came in the window. It made a warm spot on the book. "Sss sun!" said Brielle. Mom laughed. "You found two," she said.

Brielle hunted for more. She looked under the cushion. She looked in the basket. Then she wiggled her toes in her toy box of sand from the beach. "Sss sand!" she shouted. She was not mad about the mess. She was happy.

Mom helped her clean up the sand. "Sss sweep," said Mom, with a wink.

"I found S everywhere," said Brielle. She hugged her book.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Morning is the part of the day when we wake up and eat breakfast.
story:
Kayden woke up in his bed. The sun was up too. He heard spoons clink in the kitchen.

He ran to the kitchen. Mom was there. Dad was there. His big sister was eating eggs.

"Good morning, Kayden!" said Mom.

"Good morning," said Kayden. He sat down. Mom gave him toast. "Morning is when we wake up and eat breakfast," his sister said, with milk on her chin.

Kayden looked out the window. A plane went by, high in the sky. "Plane!" he said, and pointed.

Yesterday Kayden had wanted to fly a kite. But yesterday the rain came, so they stayed inside. He had started to cry. Mom had hugged him and said, "Not today. We can try tomorrow."

Today the sky was bright and blue. "Is it tomorrow now?" Kayden asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Yesterday is done. Today is now. Later we can go to the park."

"Later?" asked Kayden.

"After breakfast," said Mom. "First we eat. Then we fly your kite."

Kayden ate his toast fast. He was a little shy of the big kite pulling in the wind, so Dad held his hand.

The kite went up, up, up. It flew by the clouds, just like a plane.

"Now?" asked Kayden.

"Now!" said Dad, and the string tugged in Kayden's hand.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
fact: We smell with our nose.
story:
Elizabeth lived on a farm with her grandma. One morning grandma said, "Let's play the senses game." Elizabeth wanted to win, but she did not know all the answers yet.

Grandma held up a red apple. "What do you call this sense?" she asked. "Seeing!" said Elizabeth. "And you see with your eyes." Grandma rang a big black bell. "Hearing," said Elizabeth. "I hear with my ears." She petted a soft lamb. "Touching! I touch with my hands." Then grandma gave her warm bread. "Tasting. I taste with my mouth," said Elizabeth, and she took a big bite.

"One sense left," said grandma. She pointed to the rose garden. Elizabeth ran to the pink roses. She sniffed one, then another. The little white one smelled best of all. "Smelling!" she shouted. "We smell with our nose!" Grandma laughed and clapped. Elizabeth picked the white rose and put it on grandma's hat. "Now you smell sweet too," she said.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
fact: A grown-up should check that the water is warm, not hot, before you wash.
story:
Sadie was at summer camp. It was time for snack. The teacher said, "Wash your hands first." Sadie ran to the small sink. She wanted to wash all by herself.

Sadie turned the tap. The water came out. She put one finger near it. It felt very hot. She pulled her finger back. "Teacher Sam!" she called. "Please check my water."

Teacher Sam came over. He put his hand under the water. "It is too hot," he said. He turned the tap the other way. He put his hand under again. "Now it is warm," he said. "Warm is just right."

Sadie put her hands in the water. It felt good. She took the soap. She rubbed and rubbed. The class sang the hand song. It was a long song. "This song takes twenty seconds," said Teacher Sam. Sadie kept rubbing until the song was done. Bubbles covered her hands.

She rinsed the bubbles off. Then she got her snack. The crackers tasted good. After snack, it was nap time. Sadie lay down on her mat. "I can wash my hands now," she whispered. "All by myself." Then she closed her eyes to sleep.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
fact: Rinsing under the water washes the soap off your hands.
story:
Ryan was at summer camp. Lunchtime was coming. The camp man, Ben, called everyone to the sink. "Soap first," said Ben. "Rub for twenty seconds. Then rinse."

Ryan rubbed the soap on his hands. One, two, three. He counted to twenty. His hands felt slippery and bubbly. He ran them under the water. The water washed the soap off. Now his hands were not slippery at all. They felt clean.

Ben held out the sandwiches. But Milo's hands were still soapy. "Feel my hands," said Milo. They were slippery. Ryan pointed to the sink. "Rinse again," said Ryan. "The water washes the soap off." Milo rinsed and rinsed. His hands were clean too.

Milo smiled. "Thank you, Ryan. That was polite." The boys sat down together. Ryan took a big bite of his sandwich.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: In English, we write from left to right across the page.
story:
Lucas sat at the kitchen table. He had a big pencil and white paper. He wanted to write his name.

Mama sat next to him. "Show me the L," she said. Lucas gripped the pencil tight. "One, two, three, letters," he said. "L, U, C!"

He began at the right side of the page. He drew a big L. Then a U. Then the C went squish, right off the edge. Lucas frowned. "No room, Mama!"

Mama turned the paper around. "Try here," she said, pointing to the left side. Lucas looked. The whole long page stretched out in front of his letters.

He started at the left edge now. One L, smooth and beautiful. One U, round like a cup. One C, curvy like the moon. All the letters went across the page, one after another, left to right.

"LUCAS!" he shouted. The letters fit! They did not fall off the paper at all.

Mama clapped her hands. Lucas picked up the paper. He held it up high and grinned.

"I can write it again!" he said, and grabbed a fresh page.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Up and down are opposites.
story:
Bennett ran to the park. He wanted to be a rocket today. Rockets go up, up, up.

First he found a big red slide. Next to it was a small blue slide. His dad gave him a cold juice box from the cooler. "Brr, cold," said Bennett. His dad held a hot cup of coffee. "Hot," said Dad. "I hold it, not you."

Bennett saw the tall ladder. "Rockets climb up," he said. He put one foot on the ladder. Up he went, one step at a time, slow like a snail. At the top he shouted, "Up and down are opposites!"

Then a fast puppy ran by. It looked up at Bennett and wagged its tail. Bennett sat down. Whoosh! He slid straight down, fast like a rocket.

The puppy licked his shoe. It climbed the little steps of the small slide. Down it came, tail first.

"Again!" said Bennett.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: Everyone helps clean up the toys they played with.
story:
Addison played at Grandma's house. She built a big tower of blocks. She sent one block sliding across the rug. Then she sent another one. Soon blocks were all over the floor.

Grandma called, "Time for a snack!" Addison jumped up. She ran to the kitchen. Grandma gave her a tasty apple slice. Addison ate it all up. Then she looked back at the door. The blocks were still on the floor. Grandma had not played with them. Addison had.

Addison went back to the playroom. She picked up a block. She put it in the basket. Then another block, and another. Her bottom sat down on the rug as she reached the last ones. The floor was clear. Grandma peeked in and smiled. "All clean," said Grandma. Addison clapped her hands and patted the empty basket.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: A tablet runs out of power after being used and needs charging.
story:
Josephine went to Rosa's house. Rosa had a tablet. Rosa's mom said, "You can draw on it." Josephine looked at the black screen. She did not know what to do. "How do I make it wake up?" she asked. Rosa pushed the little round button with one finger. The screen lit up. Josephine tried it too. Tap. The screen woke up. She smiled big.

Rosa showed her the drawing app. It was a little pink square with a crayon on it. Josephine tapped it. Colors filled the screen. She picked the thin green pen. She drew a long, wiggly snake. Then she drew a red sun. "My snake is winning the race," she said. Rosa laughed and drew a fast rabbit.

Then the screen went black. Josephine's snake was gone. Her tummy felt tight. "Oh no," she said. "Did I break it?" Rosa's mom came over. "No, it just ran out of power," she said. "It needs charging." She plugged the charger into the wall. The screen showed a small battery. Josephine waited. Soon the picture came back. Her snake was still there.

Rosa's mom said, "All done for now. Let's put it away." Josephine pressed the button. The screen went dark. She laid the tablet on the soft rug, face up. Rosa's mom set it by the charger. "You learned a lot today," Rosa said. Josephine nodded. "Tap to wake. Tap to draw. And it sleeps when the power is all gone." Rosa's mom plugged in the charger and said, "Snack time, girls."

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Colors come in lighter and darker kinds, like light blue and dark blue, and both are still called blue.
story:
Weston ran to the big tree in his backyard. He wanted to find blue things for his blue box. He found a blue jay feather. He put it in the box. He found a blue bottle cap. He put that in too.

Then he found a small toy car. It was very dark blue. Weston frowned. "Is this blue?" he asked. His sister Mia ran over. "No! That is too dark!" she said.

Weston held the feather by the car. Both looked blue to him. He put them side by side in the grass. The feather was light blue. The car was dark blue. "They are both blue," he said. Mia leaned down and looked. "Oh! Light blue and dark blue!" she said. She clapped her hands. Weston put the car in the box. Then he found something new. A green leaf sat on a red wagon. "Mia! Come see!" he called. "Which green is this one?"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Today is the day that is happening right now.
story:
Sophie sat at the dinner table. She looked at her spoon. "Mom," she said, "is today the library day?"

Mom smiled. "Yes. Today is the day that is happening right now. And right now we are eating dinner. So we go after dinner."

Sophie tapped her cup. "Yesterday we went to the park," she said. "Yesterday is not now."

"That's right," said Mom. "Yesterday is done. Today is here."

Sophie ate one pea. Then she ate another. The clock ticked slowly. She reached for the bread, but it was far away. Dad passed it to her.

"Can we go now?" she asked.

"Not yet. First we eat. Later we go."

Sophie waited. She looked out the window. The last light was soft and pink. She saw the flower on the table, a yellow one in a little jar.

At last Mom stood up. "Now we go," Mom said.

Sophie jumped down from her chair. She held Mom's hand at the door.

"Today is my day," said Sophie.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: Carry a pencil with the point facing down so it cannot poke anyone.
story:
Jackson sat at the kitchen table. Mom gave him a big yellow pencil. "Now you can write your name," she said. Jackson was so happy. He jumped up and ran to show Dad. The pencil waved up in his hand, point out. Mom caught his arm gently. "Point down," she said. Jackson looked. He turned the pencil so the point faced down. He held it tight like that all the way to the door.

Then Jackson sat back down. He gripped the pencil low, near the tip. He made a shaky J. He made a wobbly a. Some letters missed the paper and went on the table. Mom wiped a wet cloth over it. "Try again," she said. Jackson tried again and again. Then he saw it. "JACKSON," all in a row. He held the paper up high. "I did it, Mom! Look!"

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: After a visit ends, families can stay in touch with phone calls, video calls or letters.
story:
Grandma came to stay for a whole week! Sienna jumped up and down. "One, two, three hugs!" she counted.

They made pancakes. Dad held the hot pan. Sienna watched and stirred the bowl. They read stories. They drew a big truck with crayons. Sienna wore her itchy new sweater to show Grandma. It was the best week ever.

Then Grandma had to go home. Sienna stood at the door. Her eyes were wet. "I will miss you," she said.

"You can call me on the phone," said Grandma. "Or we can see each other on a video call. Or you can send me a letter!"

"A letter?" said Sienna.

She ran to the table. She drew the truck. She drew Grandma. Mom helped her mail it.

Three days later, the phone rang. It was Grandma! "Your letter came!" she said. "I love my truck picture. Want a video call tomorrow?"

"Yes!" said Sienna. "One, two, three, four, five o'clock?"

"Five o'clock," laughed Grandma. "See you then!"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Yesterday is the day before today.
story:
Arlo ran to the park today. Yesterday the big slide was wet. Today the sun made it dry. "Now I can slide!" said Arlo.

A girl named Mia was at the swing. "I went to this park tomorrow," she said. Then she stopped. She thought hard. "No, not tomorrow. I went yesterday. Yesterday is the day before today." Arlo nodded. "Yesterday the slide was wet," he said. "Today it is dry."

Mia had a small red ball. She threw it high. The ball went up, and then it came down. It rolled under a bench. Arlo went to grab it. The ball was stuck. He tried once. He tried twice. Then Mia helped. Together they pulled it out. "Now we can play," said Mia.

"Can you come back tomorrow?" asked Arlo. "Yes," said Mia. "Tomorrow is the day after today." Arlo smiled. Tomorrow they would play again. At home, Arlo drew the park at his little desk. He drew Mia's red ball, and a snowy hill he would slide down some day. Then Mama called, "Dinner later, Arlo!" Arlo got one more crayon and drew the slide. "See you tomorrow, slide," he said.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
fact: In Japan, people say 'itadakimasu' before eating to give thanks for the food.
story:
Matteo went to the temple with Grandma. The bell rang once. The wood smelled like rain. People bowed and folded their hands. Matteo bowed too, just a little.

After the visit, Grandma took him to a small room. Rice and soup were on the table. Grandma put her hands together. "We say itadakimasu before we eat," she said. "In Japan, everyone says it. It gives thanks for the food." Matteo tried. "Ita... daki?" The word felt bumpy in his mouth, like his shoes bumping the table leg. "One more try," said Grandma. He tried again. "Itadaki... masu?" "Almost," said Grandma. She smiled and waited.

Matteo looked at the rice. He looked at his hands. He folded them like Grandma. He took a big breath. "Itadakimasu!" he said. Grandma clapped softly. "Just right," she said. "Now we can eat." The rice was warm. The soup was salty. Matteo ate it all up.

Later, Matteo drew a picture with a red crayon. He drew the temple. He drew Grandma. He drew a big bowl of rice. On the top he wrote some wiggly letters. "That says itadakimasu," he told Grandma. Grandma hung it on the wall. "What a lucky wall," she said. Matteo laughed. Then he folded his hands and said it one more time, all by himself.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A tiny new plant poking up out of the soil is called a sprout.
story:
Maverick dug a small hole in the dirt. He dropped in one seed. Then he patted the soil down flat. "Now grow, little seed," he said. Every day he came back. He looked and looked. No green. No leaf. Nothing at all.

"Maybe my seed is lost," said Maverick. Miss Ada, the garden helper, gave him a little stick of wood to mark his spot. "Water it, then wait," she said. Maverick gave the seed a drink. The sun made the dirt warm, but not too hot. He waited. One day, two days, three days, four days. Still nothing.

On day five, Maverick bent down low. Something green was poking up. It was very small. It looked like a tiny curl. "Miss Ada! Come quick!" he called. Miss Ada knelt beside him. "That is a sprout," she said. "A tiny new plant poking up is called a sprout." Maverick grinned. He slipped his finger next to it, soft and slow. "Hello, sprout," he whispered.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use.
story:
Eliana went to the store with Mama. She wanted to pick the apples. "Stay close to my cart," said Mama. Eliana held the side of the cart. One hand, two hands, hold on tight.

They walked past the bakery. It smelled warm and sweet. "The oven is very hot," said Mama. "The baker uses big gloves. We watch from here." Eliana saw the baker pull out bread. The bread was hot. The milk by the door was cold. Eliana touched the cold milk jug. Brrr.

Then Eliana saw something on the floor. It was small. It was a lighter. She counted to herself, one, two, three steps back. She did not touch it.

"Mama, I see a lighter," she said.

The kind store man came over. He picked it up. "Good job telling me," he said. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use." He put it in his pocket, far away.

Later a doctor came in to shop. She had a clean white coat. She smiled at Eliana.

At home, Mama washed the apples. "You were my big helper," she said.

Eliana bit her apple. Crunch.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: A clock shows what time it is.
story:
Emilia stood at the park gate. "Is it time to swing now?" she asked.

"Now it is," said Mom. "Today we can swing. Yesterday it rained, so we stayed home."

Emilia ran to the swings. She pumped her legs. The swing went up, up, up. "The swing is big now!" she said.

After swinging, Emilia wanted a turn on the slide. But a boy was there. "Can I go later?" she asked Mom.

"Yes, later, when he is done," said Mom.

Emilia waited. She watched the boy slide down. Then it was her turn. "Now it is my turn!" she said. Down she went, fast.

Then Emilia looked around. "Where did the sun go?" she asked. The sky was getting dark at the edge.

"It is almost time to go home," said Mom. Mom held up her phone. A clock was on it. "Look. The clock shows what time it is."

Emilia looked at the clock. "Will we come back?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Tomorrow we will come back. It will be a beautiful summer day again."

Emilia smiled. She held Mom's hand. "Swing tomorrow?" she asked.

"Swing tomorrow," said Mom. They walked home together.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
fact: Your skin can feel whether something is soft or rough.
story:
Grayson walked on the nature trail with his mom. He found a small purple feather on the ground. He picked it up. "This is a puzzle," he said. "Some things feel different."

His mom smiled. "Your hands can tell," she said. Grayson touched the feather. It felt soft. He put it in the soft pile.

Then he found a pinecone. He touched it. The pinecone felt bumpy and rough. He put it in the rough pile. His mom held out a small blanket from the bag. Grayson rubbed it with his fingers. "Soft," he said. It went in the soft pile too.

"Now close your eyes," said Mom. Grayson closed his eyes. She put something in his hands. His skin felt little bumps. "Rough!" he said. He opened his eyes. It was the pinecone.

Grayson laughed and held the soft feather to his cheek.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: At the beach, a child goes near the water only with a grown-up watching.
story:
Hannah sat on the train with Mama. The window made a whoosh sound. Trees went by, fast. Hannah held her little pig toy. "We are going to the sea," said Mama. "The sea has big water."

The train stopped. Then the train went again. Hannah looked and looked. At last they got off. The sand was warm under Hannah's feet. Far away, the water went splash, splash. Hannah wanted to run to it now.

She started to run. "Wait," said Mama. "At the beach, a child goes near the water only with a grown-up watching. Let me put down the bag first." Hannah stopped. She waited. She held her pig and watched the waves. They went up and down, up and down.

Mama put down the bag. Mama took Hannah's hand. They walked to the water together. The water was cool on Hannah's toes. It splashed her pig too. "Same wet toes, same wet pig!" said Hannah. Mama laughed and held her hand tight.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: Many libraries ask people to use quiet voices so others can read.
story:
Lydia stood in the reading corner. She was holding something new. It was her very first library card.

"I want a dinosaur book!" she shouted. A boy next to her looked up. He pointed at the big rug. Two kids were reading there. One had a book about bears. The other had a book about the moon.

The librarian bent down. "We use quiet voices here," she said softly. "So others can read." Lydia looked at the kids on the rug. Then she whispered, "A dinosaur book, please." The librarian smiled and whispered back, "Top shelf, little friend."

Lydia found a big green dinosaur book. She carried it with two hands. At the desk, she gave her card. Beep! The librarian scanned the book. "All yours for now," she whispered.

Lydia clapped her hands, very quietly. "A tiny clap," she said with a giggle. "For a big dinosaur." The boy next to her laughed. "Tiny clap for a T. rex," he whispered. Lydia hugged her book and tiptoed to the door. "Bye, library," she sang in a small, small voice.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Dogs, cows and fish are all animals.
story:
It was animal day at school. Weston brought his toy fish to show. His friend Ben brought a toy dog. Mia brought a toy cow.

"Your fish is not an animal," said Ben. "It has no legs. My dog has legs. Mia's cow has legs."

Weston felt sad. He wanted his fish to count. Miss Rosa said, "Let's look at the animal wall." The wall was full of pictures. Weston saw a dog there. He saw a cow there. Then he saw a fish there, too!

"Dogs, cows and fish are all animals," said Miss Rosa. Weston smiled big. "My fish is an animal!" he said.

Then it was snack time. Miss Rosa gave out foods. There were apples and crackers. Weston took a bite of his apple. Then he held his fish up high.

"Fish can swim," he said. "Dogs and cows cannot swim like that."

Ben listened. "My dog can swim a little," he said. "But not like a fish."

The class sat on the floor. They lined up all the animals in a row. Dog, cow, fish, dog, cow, fish. Weston counted them one by one.

Then came the surprise. Miss Rosa opened a box. A real bunny was inside! "This is an animal, too," she said. Weston laughed and clapped. "Animals, animals, everywhere!"

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: Cutting a square from one corner to the opposite corner makes two triangles.
story:
Sofia went to the library with her dad. She saw a circle rug on the floor. She saw square books on the shelf. A song was playing, and some kids began to clap.

At the craft table, Sofia wanted to make a paper sailboat. She needed two triangle sails. She looked in the paper box. She found only one square paper. "Where can I get triangles?" she asked. Miss Amy, the librarian, came over. "Bring the square here," she said. Miss Amy took the scissors. She cut from one corner to the opposite corner. The square fell open in Sofia's hands. Two triangles!

Sofia held one triangle up. Then she held the other up. Her loose tooth wiggled when she smiled. She taped both triangles to her boat. "Look, Dad! My boat has two sails!" Dad clapped for her. Sofia put her boat on the circle rug and gave it a little push.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Now means at this very moment.
story:
Eleanor sat at the dinner table. She folded her napkin into a little square. "Dad, is the story time now?" she asked.

Dad stirred the pot. "The story is not now. The story is after dinner."

Eleanor looked at her plate. The carrots were still there. She ate one. Then she ate another. "Is it now?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Dad. "Now you are eating carrots. Later we will read."

Eleanor ate slow. She watched Dad take the pot off the stove. He poured the soup carefully. Eleanor waited. She folded her napkin again.

"Now?" she asked.

"Now," said Dad.

Eleanor was brave about the hot bowl. She let it cool while Dad sat down. Yesterday they had soup too. Tomorrow they would have pasta. Today was soup day, and story day.

After the last spoonful, Dad wiped her chin. "Is it after dinner now?" Eleanor asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "It is now story time."

Eleanor ran to get her book. Dad patted the chair beside him. Eleanor climbed up and opened the cover.

"Now," she whispered, and Dad began to read.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Adding white paint to a color makes it lighter, so red with white becomes pink.
story:
Madeline went to the park with Daddy. She wanted to make a card for Grandma. The card needed a pink flower. "I only have red paint," said Daddy. Madeline made a sad face.

First she played on the swing. Daddy pushed her high, high, high. "One, two, three," she counted. Then she saw a green frog by the pond. She saw a blue bird up in a tree. She saw a yellow duck waddle by. "Green frog, blue bird, yellow duck," she said.

Then a girl named Bella sat at the paint table. Bella had white paint. Madeline had red paint. "Let's mix," said Bella. Madeline stirred white into her red paint. She stirred and stirred. "Pink!" she yelled. Red and white made pink. It was pink, pink, pink!

Madeline painted a pink flower on the card. She helped Bella fold the card into a square. "For Grandma," said Madeline. "You did it," said Daddy. He gave her a big hug.

Madeline ran to the car. She held the pink flower card up high. "Pink flower for Grandma!"
